title: Living witness
passages:
The service rig's drive tires bit the drainage shoulder's loose gravel, fishtailing once before Ospina caught it. They'd run 7-K hard from Kettering — two hundred klicks of washboard haul road with the chipped die warm in their coat pocket and Kass's badge 2241 burning a hole in the named-rider slot. The unmarked cradle rig sat square across the lane ahead, Pell's silhouette black against the work lights spilling from Anza's ore siding.

Ospina didn't brake. They clipped the cradle rig's rear corner at thirty klicks, a sound like a shipping container dropped from a crane. Metal screamed. 7-K's bumper folded. The cradle rig slewed sideways, its stabilizers digging furrows in the hardpan.

"Channel holding," Kass said. Their voice came tight through the named-rider link, backgrounded by the dish array's proximity alarm — a rising whine that meant the comms mast was three seconds from auto-fold. "Near-end warning. Two minutes to line-of-sight loss."

Ospina killed 7-K's momentum with a jab of the retarder, swung the nose into the siding's unlit throat. The ore stub's switch lights showed red over red. Dead track. Good. They'd have to come on foot.

"Pell's moving," Kass said. "He's turning his rig. Coming in behind us."

The dish screamed its final warning and folded. The named-rider channel dropped to carrier-wave only — no voice, no data, just a heartbeat ping that meant *alive, waiting*. Kass's fingers never left the console.

Ospina killed 7-K's engine. Silence rushed in, thick with dust and the smell of hot hydraulic fluid. They palmed the door release, stepped down into the siding's shadow. The chipped die pressed against their ribs through the coat lining. One corner chipped, the pattern shifted. The forger's own tool. The only thing that could unmake what the forger had made.

Ahead, the relay shop's floodlights cut a rectangle across the yard. Teodoro stood in the doorway, dispatch line in one hand, pod plate in the other. At the med rig's flank, Rhea's hand rested on seal K-7745, winch cable slack. Marlowe sat on the rig's lower step, shoulder braced, watching the siding mouth.

Pell's cradle rig crunched into the siding behind them, tires grinding ballast. Its door threw open.

Ospina didn't turn. They walked toward the shop, boots loud on the ties. Let him follow. The die in their pocket was the only warrant that mattered now.

Inside the shop the node board was arguing with itself.

It was a laminate slab the size of a door, bolted over the shift rack, and it ran Anza the way a pulse runs a body: crew, cargo, resupply windows, all of it in green line type Teodoro retyped by hand whenever the uplink dropped, which was most days. At the top of the crew block, fresh enough that the letters still carried chalk dust:

MARLOWE, D. — ENTERED BY RHEA, MECHANIC, SHIFT 1

Under it, blinking at half a second: PENDING COUNTERSIGN.

"That's the field," Teodoro said. He didn't look up. He had the fresh scrubber cartridge in his fist, a gray canister the size of a beer can packed with granules that pull the carbon dioxide out of a man's breath and hold onto it, and his eyes stayed on the respirator gauge instead. *00:37.* "Line's rule. Anything one node enters on its own authority is a rumor until a registered seal authority punches it. Somebody whose die is on file with the line's desk. Otherwise it's a name somebody felt like typing."

"Then punch it," Rhea said.

"Nobody at Anza holds a die." He said it fast, the way he said everything, all of it free and none of it asked for. "Nearest is Kettering, Bay 4 seal authority, V. Ospina, Shift 2, four hundred ten klicks. After that, Ceres Flats, five sixty. And the board runs a turnover scrub at 06:00 — any crew line without a countersign comes off as unlogged. That's how people walk out of here and never get counted. Not drama. Housekeeping."

Rhea hit the diagnostic key with the flat of her hand. The board re-read the pod plate, thought about it, and printed: ENTRY VALID — MECHANIC AUTHORITY — AWAITING COUNTERSIGN.

"There," she said. "It says he's crew."

"It said I was four hundred twelve kilos of ballast," Marlowe said, "and a reclaimer read it out loud in front of the whole shop."

"Different plate."

"Same box, Rhea."

She got him off the med rig's lower step with two fingers hooked in his collar, which he allowed, being one-armed. "Crew stands at the board. Try not to fall over on the node's laminate."

"Do I salute it?"

"You can start by not bleeding on it."

Under the mask Ivo made a sound that was almost a laugh and cost him air. *00:31.*

"Thirty-one," Teodoro said, to nobody. "When it zeroes I break the seal and seat the new one, and he holds his breath for a fifteen count while I do it. Diaphragm's patched with glove rubber, so it leaks. Fifteen is the number. Sixteen and he's on the floor."

"Then don't spend the fifteen watching me type," Rhea said, and typed nothing, because there was nothing to type. Her hand sat on the board's edge. "Can I countersign?"

"You can sign. Board takes your name, logs the refusal, hands you the same blinking field. And Pell reads refusals for a living." Teodoro finally looked up. "You want a seal, not a mechanic."

"Twenty-two," said Ivo, muffled.

Boots came up the ties outside, unhurried, no light with them.

"That's not Pell," Teodoro said. "Pell's rig is heavier."

The doorway filled with dust and a person in a Kettering coat, one hand in the pocket. Ospina looked at the crew block, at the blinking field, at Marlowe standing crooked under it with his shoulder braced wrong.

"V. Ospina," they said. "Bay 4 seal authority. Somebody around here type my name?"

"Eleven," Teodoro said, and the respirator clicked over onto its reserve.

Miko's boots found the stub switch ties before her breath did. The switch stand was a steel skeleton bolted to the ballast, its throw lever frozen in the diverge position — red over red, dead track both ways. Doan stood at the overlap locker ten meters down, the key already turning in the hasp. They didn't look back. Their wrist cord dangled from the locker handle where they'd left it, the coiled tether bright against the rust.

"Don't," Miko said. Her voice came out ragged, steam in the cold. "Doan. Stop."

Doan's shoulders hitched once. The locker door swung wide. "Shift change in three minutes. Nour signed the tally. I'm just — "

"Just what? Feeding the line?" Miko closed the distance in three long strides, grabbed the wrist cord's free end, and yanked. The locker door slammed shut on the hasp, the key trapped halfway turned. Doan stumbled back, wrist caught in the cord's loop, and fetched up against the switch stand's cross brace.

"Let go."

"Open it. Slow. Show me what's inside."

Doan's face went flat. The kind of flat that meant they'd run the numbers and didn't like the answer. "You don't want this, Miko. You *really* don't."

"I want to know why the seal locker counted short. I want to know why Nour's name is on the authorization. And I want to know why you're running for the stub switch with the overlap key when Pell's reclaimer is twenty meters behind us." She held the cord taut, one hand on the locker handle. "Open it."

Doan's jaw worked. They reached up with their free hand, fingers finding the hasp, and forced the key the rest of the way. The locker exhaled — cold air, machine oil, the dry scent of desiccant packs.

Miko leaned in, cord still tight. The seal tray was a molded foam insert cut for forty dies. Thirty-eight cavities sat empty. Two held tags: yellow plastic, hand-stamped *BAY 4 / SHIFT 2* in faded ink, the numbers rubbed half away by thumb and forefinger.

"Thirty-eight," she said. "Thirty-eight seals gone. All Bay 4."

"Resupply arrangement," Doan said, quiet now. "Kettering sends us food, medical, scrubber granules — we send them seals. Dies. Authority. Nour negotiated it three winters back. Anza stays fat on the schedule. Kettering gets sealing capacity they lost when their Bay 4 press failed."

"And the loaders? The people you crimp into pods and ship as ballast?"

Doan didn't answer. Their eyes tracked past Miko's shoulder, up the siding toward the shop floodlights where a second rig's engine had just cut.

"Pell," they said. "He's here. He heard Nour on open channel. He knows about the arrangement. He'll take the seals, the loader, the *hands* — "

"Hands?"

"The second pair. The one who held the lid and counted down." Doan's voice cracked. "Nour knows who. She won't say. But Pell will make her."

Miko's grip on the cord slackened. The tags in the tray caught the switch stand's amber tell-tale, *BAY 4 / SHIFT 2* winking like a warning.

"Who counted down, Doan?"

The switch stand's relay clicked. Somewhere down the line, a signal changed.

"Doan," Miko said. "Who held the lid?"

Doan's mouth opened. Then their head snapped toward the shop, toward the sound of heavy boots on metal grating — two sets, not one — and the unmistakable *chunk* of a warrant-token seating in a board reader.

"Too late," Doan said. "He's at the board. He's freezing it."

Miko released the cord. Doan didn't run. They stood there, wrist still looped, staring at the two empty tags in a tray built for forty, while the shop's floodlights painted their face in green and white.

Pell came up the grating without a light and went to the board first, not to any of them.

The warrant-token was a dull brass slab, palm-sized, heavy at the end where the keyway sat. He seated it in the reader under the crew block with the ease of a man who had done it four hundred times, and the board took it with a sound like a ratchet taking up slack. Every green line on the laminate went amber.

RESUPPLY HELD — LINE RECLAMATION — ANZA RELAY.

Under that, itemized, because the line itemized everything: forty scrubber cartridges, six boxes broad-spectrum, twelve intake filters, the salt, the winter diesel allocation.

"Forty," Teodoro said. His fist tightened on the gray canister. The rest came out fast and free, the way everything came out of him. "That's ten weeks at Ivo's draw. Eleven if he sleeps sitting up, which he does. And when the hold lifts the drop doesn't backfill, it re-keys to the next node in the queue, and the next node is Ceres Flats, and Ceres is already short, so it doesn't come back at all. That's not a threat. That's the queue."

"I didn't write the queue," Pell said. "I read it."

He turned around. Dust to the knee, one glove torn at the thumb, a scrape over his eye that had stopped bleeding and gone tacky. He didn't look at Ospina. He didn't look at Marlowe. He looked at the space a hand's width above Marlowe's head, the way you look at a shelf.

"Derelict discrepancy. Kettering, Bay 4, Shift 2. One unit, four hundred twelve kilos, entered as ballast, discharged 21:47. Hold is live to turnover." He tapped the token's keyway. "At 06:00 this node scrubs, anything without a countersign comes off as unlogged, and I load the discrepancy onto my cradle and haul it down the line where it can be closed quiet."

"He's standing right there," Rhea said.

"I don't talk to cargo."

"He asked you what ballast meant."

"And I answered. Twelve words. More courtesy than the line requires."

"Nineteen," Marlowe said.

Pell's jaw stopped for a second, then started again. "The hands are next on my sheet. Bay 4, Shift 2, the pair that held the lid and counted. That's a separate claim and it doesn't need this one to close, so nobody in this room should get clever about protecting them."

Ospina stepped into the floodlight rectangle and let it have their coat, the Kettering flash, the empty pocket hanging open. "V. Ospina. Bay 4 seal authority, Shift 2. Your reader can ask."

The token asked. Amber type crawled up the laminate, three lines, a registry number Ospina had been staring at for two hundred klicks.

Pell read it twice. Something moved behind his face that wasn't quite surprise, more like a column adding up wrong. "That die is in my discrepancy."

"That die is in my coat."

"Then we want the same object." He put one gloved finger on the crew block, under the blinking field. "Here's the standing order, and I'll say it once, loud, so the board has it. A living witness countersigned by a live seal authority travels as crew. Crew I cannot haul. Weight I can. So the node has until turnover to put two marks on this line, or the box goes back down the haul road with me and nobody counts what happens to it after that."

"That's a hell of a thing to hand us," Rhea said.

"It's not a favor, it's an order, and I'm bound by it same as you. I'd rather have the box." Pell stepped back from the board and folded his arms. "Entering mechanic signs the crew entry. Seal authority strikes the seal field. Both in front of me, both before the scrub."

"00:19," Teodoro said. The respirator clicked, hunting for a breath that wasn't in the reservoir. "Rhea. *Rhea.*"

Rhea put her hand flat on the board's edge, over the amber, over her own name in chalk dust. "And when the seal comes down?"

"When the seal comes down, seal authority," Pell said, "that die leaves the pocket and goes into my evidence sleeve, because it's the tool that closed my discrepancy and I don't lose tools."

Ospina's hand went into the coat. Their thumb found the chipped corner, the one that shifted the pattern.

"Sign, mechanic," Pell said.
